summary:
OrVitals is an intelligent health monitoring platform designed to help astronauts stay healthy and safe during long-duration space missions.

Space exploration exposes astronauts to unique health risks, including microgravity, radiation, isolation, and physiological stress. Monitoring these risks becomes especially important during missions to the Moon and Mars, where immediate medical assistance from Earth may not be available.

Our solution aims to centralize essential health indicators, such as heart rate, sleep quality, physical activity, and psychological well-being, in an intuitive dashboard. By visualizing health trends, highlighting potential anomalies, and providing actionable insights, OrVitals helps astronauts better understand their physical and mental condition and make informed decisions.

Our goal is to transform complex health data into accessible, meaningful information, enabling more autonomous health management and contributing to safer, more sustainable human space exploration.
details:
Our project is a mission monitoring prototype that brings spacecraft telemetry and astronaut health observations into one system. Our aim is to help crews understand changing conditions and investigate unusual readings, with local forecasting that does not require a remote AI service.

The working demonstration simulates oxygen pressure, cabin temperature, and battery charge. Independent devices publish measurements over MQTT, and a browser monitor displays live readings, charts, device status, and message traffic. Users can filter the stream and export readings as JSON.

A separate ingestion pipeline validates incoming measurements, queues them through NATS JetStream, stores time series in PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB, caches recent values in Redis, and archives raw messages in S3-compatible storage. The backend also supports health observations, user preferences, and saved dashboard layouts.

Our machine learning package uses 60 consecutive measurements to predict the next 10 values. It compares Ridge regression with a temporal convolutional network and combines forecasting errors with Isolation Forest anomaly detection. Exported ONNX models run locally on CPU. We evaluate forecasting accuracy, prediction intervals, and detection of simulated faults such as spikes, drift, and stuck sensors.

The creative idea is to combine automatic sensor readings, personal observations, and local predictions within a customizable mission workspace. The intended benefit is better awareness of conditions during missions where connectivity may be limited.

We developed the prototype using TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Bun, Elysia, MQTT.js, Eclipse Mosquitto, Docker Compose, and Drizzle ORM. The ML package uses NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch, and ONNX Runtime. A Next.js and React frontend scaffold provides the starting point for the planned dashboard.

We considered data provenance, irregular measurements, disconnected devices, false alarms, reproducible evaluation, and the distinction between simulated readings and actual mission data. All current telemetry and training data are synthetic. The ML package runs independently and is not yet connected to live ingestion. The integrated dashboard remains future work; the current visualization is the MQTT monitor. This is a software prototype, with no physical spacecraft sensors or validated medical decision support.
